p.src: Hearing this, the demon king thought to himself, “My father has always lived on human flesh and is now well over a thousand years old. How has he suddenly taken to fasting? After all the evil he committed in the past, how could three or four days of abstinence possibly make amends? There is something false in his words. Suspicious indeed!” He immediately withdrew to the second gate, summoned the Six Stalwart Commanders, and asked, “Where did you invite the old king from?” The little demons replied, “We met and invited him on the way.” The demon king said, “I thought you had returned remarkably quickly. You never reached his home?” The little demons said, “That is right; we did not.” The demon king said, “This is bad—we have fallen for his imposture. That is not the old king.” The little demons all knelt and said, “Your Majesty, can you not even recognize your own father?” The demon king said, “His appearance and every movement are alike; only his speech is not. I fear he is an impostor and that we shall suffer at his hands. You must all be watchful: those who wield sabres, draw them; those who wield spears, polish their points bright. Let the staff-wielders take up their staffs and the rope-wielders their ropes. I shall go and question him again to see what he says. If he truly is the old king, what harm would there be if we waited a month, let alone abstaining today and tomorrow? But if his words do not tally, the moment you hear me grunt, all strike together.” The demons each accepted his orders.

Whatever you have to say, speak freely.” Prostrate on the ground, the demon king said, “Your foolish son invited you here first to offer you Tang Monk’s flesh, and second to ask you something. While roaming idly the other day, I rode an auspicious radiance straight up into the ninth heaven, where I unexpectedly met Master Zhang Daoling, patriarch of the Daoist tradition.” The Pilgrim said, “Do you mean Zhang Daoling, the Celestial Master?” The demon king said, “The very man.” The Pilgrim asked, “What did he say?” The demon king said, “Seeing that your son had well-proportioned features and a balanced face and figure, he asked the year, month, day, and hour of my birth. Being young, I could not remember it clearly. The master is deeply versed in Ziping astrology and wished to calculate my fate by the Five Planets. That is precisely what I wished to ask you now, Father. Should I meet him again, I could then trouble him to make the calculation.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim sat above and laughed inwardly: “What a cunning monster! Since old Monkey attained the Buddhist path and began escorting Master Tang, I have caught several monsters along the way, but never one so exacting as this fellow. Had he asked about household courtesies, family trifles, a shortage of rice, or a lack of firewood, I could readily have made up some glib answer. Sitting majestically upright in the center without the slightest look of fear, he instead smiled cheerfully and said, “Rise, worthy son. I am old, and for several days affairs have not gone as I wished, so by chance I truly forgot the hour of your birth. Wait until we return home tomorrow and ask your mother; then we shall know.”

The Great Sage straightened his robes, composed himself reverently, steadied his steps, and entered directly. On seeing the Bodhisattva, he prostrated himself in worship. He released the Samadhi Fire, and we could not defeat him or rescue our master. I hurried to the Eastern Ocean and invited the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas to bring rain, but even that could not overcome the fire. Your disciple was badly smoked and nearly lost what little life remained to him.” The Bodhisattva said, “Since his is the Samadhi Fire and his magic powers are great, why did you invite the Dragon Kings instead of coming to invite me?” The Pilgrim said, “I had intended to come, but your disciple had been overcome by smoke and could not ride a cloud, so I sent Zhu Bajie to invite the Bodhisattva.” The Bodhisattva said, “Wuneng never came.” The Pilgrim said, “Exactly. In a moment he lowered his cloud and went straight to Mount Potalaka’s cliff.
As he walked forward with solemn bearing, the devas of the twenty-four orders came to meet him and asked, “Great Sage, where are you going?”
After saluting them, the Pilgrim said, “I wish to see the Bodhisattva.”
The devas said, “Wait a moment while we announce you.”
The deva Hariti then went outside the Cave of Tidal Sound and reported, “May the Bodhisattva be informed: Sun Wukong has come especially to pay his respects.”
On hearing the report, the Bodhisattva immediately ordered that he be admitted.
The Great Sage straightened his robes, composed himself reverently, steadied his steps, and entered directly. On seeing the Bodhisattva, he prostrated himself in worship.
The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, why are you here instead of escorting the Golden Cicada to the Western Heaven to seek the scriptures?”
The Pilgrim said, “I report to the Bodhisattva: Your disciple was escorting Tang Monk onward when we reached a place called Withered-Pine Ravine on Mount Hao, where there is a Fire-Cloud Cave.
There a monster called Red Boy, who styles himself the Holy Infant Great King, carried off my master.
Your disciple, Zhu Wuneng, and the others tracked him to his gate and fought with him.
He released the Samadhi Fire, and we could not defeat him or rescue our master.

I hurried to the Eastern Ocean and invited the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas to bring rain, but even that could not overcome the fire. Your disciple was badly smoked and nearly lost what little life remained to him.”
The Bodhisattva said, “Since his is the Samadhi Fire and his magic powers are great, why did you invite the Dragon Kings instead of coming to invite me?”
The Pilgrim said, “I had intended to come, but your disciple had been overcome by smoke and could not ride a cloud, so I sent Zhu Bajie to invite the Bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva said, “Wuneng never came.”
The Pilgrim said, “Exactly.

Before he could reach your sacred mountain, the monster disguised himself as the Bodhisattva, tricked Zhu Bajie into the cave as well, and now has him hanging in a leather bag, intending to steam and eat him too.”

p.src: When the Bodhisattva heard this, she was greatly angered. “How dare that wretched demon assume my likeness?” With an angry snort, she hurled the precious pearl and the pure vase in her hands straight into the heart of the sea. My words must have displeased her and marred her virtue, so she smashed away the pure vase. What a pity, what a pity! Had I known, she might as well have given it to old Monkey. Would that not have been a splendid thing?”

p.src: The turtle carried the pure vase to the edge of the cliff, then nodded twenty-four times to the Bodhisattva, those nods serving as twenty-four bows. Seeing this, Pilgrim laughed to himself. “So it is the keeper of the vase. I suppose when the vase disappeared, she demanded it back from him.” The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, what are you muttering down there?” “Nothing,” replied Pilgrim. The Bodhisattva ordered, “Bring the vase up here.” Pilgrim at once went to take it. Alas! He could not hope to move it. He was like a dragonfly trying to shake a stone pillar—how could he budge it even the slightest fraction? Pilgrim went forward, knelt, and said, “Bodhisattva, your disciple cannot lift it.” The Bodhisattva said, “You monkey, all you can do is boast. If you cannot even lift this little vase, how will you subdue and bind demons?” Pilgrim replied, “I will not conceal the truth from you, Bodhisattva. Ordinarily I can lift it, but today I cannot. I suppose the demon has gotten the better of me and weakened my strength.” The Bodhisattva said, “Ordinarily it is an empty vase. But now that the pure vase was cast into the sea, in that brief time it passed through the Three Rivers and Five Lakes, the Eight Seas and Four Waterways, and every stream, spring, pool, and cavern, borrowing altogether the water of an entire sea into itself. How could you possess the strength to shoulder a sea? That is why you cannot lift it.” Pilgrim joined his palms and said, “Indeed. Your disciple did not know.”

p.src: The Bodhisattva stepped forward, lightly raised the pure vase with her right hand, and rested it upon her left palm. The turtle nodded its head and slipped back beneath the water. Pilgrim said, “So it was merely a lumbering servant kept to guard the vase.” When the Bodhisattva had seated herself, she said, “Wukong, the sweet dew in my vase differs from the Dragon King’s privately bestowed rain. It can extinguish that demon’s samadhi fire. I would let you take it with you, but you cannot lift it. I might send the Dragon Girl Shancai with you, but your intentions are unreliable, and you are forever deceiving people. You may see that my Dragon Girl is beautiful and that the pure vase is a treasure, and trick her away with both. Where would I find the time to hunt you down afterward? You must leave something behind as security.” Pilgrim cried, “How cruel! Bodhisattva, you are far too suspicious. Since your disciple entered the Buddhist order, I have long ceased to engage in such conduct. You tell me to leave a pledge, but what can I offer? This cotton robe I wear was itself bestowed on me by your venerable self. How many copper coins could this tiger-skin kilt be worth? As for this iron staff, I need it constantly for protection. Only this circlet on my head is made of gold, but you devised a spell that fixed it there, so I cannot remove it. Since you now require security, I am willing to pledge this. Recite a spell to loosen the circlet and take it off. Otherwise, what else can I pledge?” The Bodhisattva said, “That would suit you very well! I want neither your clothes, your iron staff, nor your golden circlet. Just pluck one of the life-saving hairs from the back of your head and leave it with me as security.” Pilgrim said, “Those hairs were also given to me by your venerable self. I fear that if I pluck out even one, I shall break up the set, and they will no longer be able to save my life.” The Bodhisattva scolded him. “You monkey! If you will not part with even a single hair, it is difficult for me to part with Shancai.” Pilgrim laughed. “Bodhisattva, you too are overly suspicious. p.src: The Great Sage Sun was overjoyed and escorted Guanyin out of the Immortal Cave of Tidal Sound. All the great celestial deities stood arrayed upon Mount Potalaka. The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, cross the sea.” Pilgrim bowed and said, “Bodhisattva, please go first.” “You go ahead,” said the Bodhisattva. Pilgrim kowtowed and said, “Your disciple would not dare display his tricks before the Bodhisattva. If I mount my somersault cloud, I shall expose my body as I vault upward, and I fear you may deem me disrespectful.” Hearing this, the Bodhisattva ordered the Dragon Girl Shancai to go to the lotus pond, split off one lotus petal, and place it on the water below the rocky cliff. She told Pilgrim, “Step onto that lotus petal, and I shall carry you across the sea.” When Pilgrim saw it, he said, “Bodhisattva, this petal is so light and thin; how could it bear my weight? If it overturns and pitches me into the water, will not my tiger-skin kilt be soaked? If the dressing washes out, how shall I wear it in the cold weather?” The Bodhisattva barked, “Just get on it and see.” Pilgrim dared not refuse and, risking his life, leapt onto it. Sure enough, though at first it had looked light and tiny, once he stood upon it, it was considerably larger than a seagoing ship. Delighted, Pilgrim said, “Bodhisattva, it can bear me after all.” The Bodhisattva said, “Since it can bear you, why do you not cross?” Pilgrim replied, “There is neither pole, oar, sail, nor mast. How am I to get across?” “You need none,” said the Bodhisattva. With one breath she made the petal open and close, then with another mighty breath blew it across the bitter southern sea until it reached the farther shore. When Pilgrim’s feet touched solid ground, he laughed and said, “The Bodhisattva is showing off her divine powers, ordering old Monkey here and there, yet it costs her no effort at all.”

He was a disciple personally instructed by the Bodhisattva, never leaving her side, and was known as Dharma-Protector Pilgrim Huian. Huian immediately joined his palms before the Bodhisattva and awaited her command. The Bodhisattva said, “Go quickly to the upper realm, see your royal father, and ask to borrow his Celestial Ladle Blades for my use.” Huian asked, “How many does Master require?” “I need the complete set,” replied the Bodhisattva.

She ordered your son to present her respects to you, Father, and borrow the Celestial Ladle Blades for her use.” The Heavenly King at once summoned Nezha, had him fetch all thirty-six blades, and hand them to Moksha. Moksha said to Nezha, “Brother, when you return, give Mother my deepest respects. My business is urgent; I shall kowtow to her after I have delivered the blades.” They hurriedly took leave of each other. Moksha brought down his auspicious radiance, went straight to the Southern Sea, and presented the blades to the Bodhisattva.

Brandishing a fist with one hand and his staff with the other, he shouted, “Monster, open the gate!” The little fiends went inside once more and reported, “Sun Wukong has come again.” The demon king said, “Bar the gate tightly and pay him no heed.” Wukong shouted, “My good son! You drove your father outside—will you still not open the gate?” The little fiends reported again, “Sun Wukong has started hurling that insult.” The demon king merely ordered, “Ignore him.” Wukong called twice, but when the gate remained shut, fury rose in his heart. He raised his iron staff and smashed a hole through the gate with a single blow. What punishment do you deserve for breaking my gate?” Wukong replied, “My son, what punishment do you deserve for driving your father out of doors?”

p.src: The demon king flushed with shame and anger, snatched up his long spear, and thrust it straight at Wukong’s chest; Wukong raised his iron staff, parried the blow, and struck back. Once they had crossed weapons and fought four or five rounds, Wukong kept his fist clenched, dragged his staff behind him, and fled in defeat. Standing before the mountain, the demon king said, “I am going to have Tang Sanzang scrubbed and prepared.” Wukong said, “My good son, Heaven is watching you. Come after me.” Hearing this, the monster grew still angrier. With a shout he charged up, leveled his spear, and thrust again; Wukong swung his staff and fought several more rounds, then again broke ranks and fled. The demon king cursed, “Monkey, before this you could hold out for twenty or thirty rounds. Why do you now flee just when the fight is well under way?” Wukong laughed. “My worthy son, your father is afraid you will breathe fire.” The monster said, “I will not use fire. Come back and fight.” Wukong said, “If you will not use fire, then come farther away. A true hero does not strike a man at his own doorstep.” Unaware of the trick, the monster actually raised his spear and gave chase again. Wukong dragged his staff behind him and unclenched his fist. The demon king fell under the spell of delusion and thought of nothing but pursuit. The one ahead sped like a shooting star across the heavens, and the one behind like a bolt loosed from a crossbow.

p.src: Before long, the Bodhisattva came into view. Wukong said, “Monster, I am afraid of you. Spare me. Now that you have chased me all the way to Guanyin Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, why do you still not turn back?” The demon king did not believe him. Gritting his teeth, he kept charging after him. Wukong gave his body a shake and hid within the radiance surrounding the Bodhisattva. The monster saw that Wukong had vanished. He drew near, opened his eyes wide, and asked the Bodhisattva, “Are you the reinforcement Sun Wukong summoned?” The Bodhisattva made no reply. The demon king twirled his long spear and shouted, “Hey! Are you the reinforcement Sun Wukong summoned?” Still the Bodhisattva gave no answer. The monster drove his spear straight at the Bodhisattva’s heart. The Bodhisattva transformed into a beam of golden light and shot straight up into the ninth heaven. p.src: At this time Wukong and Moksha were both in the air, watching side by side. They saw the monster give a cold chuckle. “You wretched monkey, you have misjudged me. He has no idea who I, the Holy Infant, am. After failing to defeat me time and again, he went off to summon some useless Bodhisattva, whom I sent vanishing without a trace with a single thrust of my spear. She even left behind her jeweled lotus throne. I think I shall climb up and have a seat.” What a monster! Imitating the Bodhisattva, he folded his hands and crossed his legs, then sat down in the center. Seeing this, Wukong said, “Fine, fine, fine! The lotus throne has been given away to someone else.” The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, what are you saying now?” Wukong replied, “What am I saying? What am I saying? The lotus throne has been given away. That monster has planted his backside upon it. Surely you cannot mean to take it back now?” The Bodhisattva said, “I wanted him to sit on it.” Wukong said, “His body is small and nimble; he sits upon it even more steadily than you did.” The Bodhisattva called, “Say no more. Just watch my power.”

p.src: She pointed the willow branch downward and cried, “Withdraw!” At once the lotus throne lost all its radiant colors and every auspicious ray vanished; the demon king was revealed sitting upon the points of the blades. She then ordered Moksha, “Use your demon-subduing cudgel and hammer down the hilts of the blades.” Moksha lowered his cloud and pounded with the demon-subduing cudgel as though ramming a wall, striking well over a thousand blows. The blades pierced straight through the demon’s two legs, their points emerging as blood poured out in pools and flesh split open. What a monster! See how he clenched his teeth and endured the pain, cast aside his spear, and seized the blades with both hands, tugging wildly at them. Pilgrim said, “Bodhisattva, that monster feels no pain—he is still pulling at the blades!” Seeing this, the Bodhisattva called Moksha back. “Do not take his life.” She lowered the willow branch once more and uttered the mantra syllable “Om.” All the Heavenly Stems’ blades turned into backward-barbed hooks, jagged like wolves’ teeth, so that none could be pulled free. Only then did the demon panic. Gripping the blade points, he cried out in agony, “Bodhisattva, I, your disciple, was blind and failed to recognize the vastness of your divine power. I beg you a thousand times to show mercy and spare my life. Never again shall I rely on wickedness; I am willing to enter the Buddhist path and observe its precepts.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Bodhisattva descended on a golden radiance with the two Pilgrims and the white parrot. Coming before the demon, she asked, “Will you accept my precepts?” The demon king nodded through falling tears. “If you spare my life, I am willing to accept the precepts.” The Bodhisattva said, “Will you enter my order?” The demon king replied, “If you truly spare my life, I am willing to enter the Buddhist path.” The Bodhisattva said, “Since that is so, I shall lay my hand upon your crown and administer the precepts.” From her sleeve she drew a small golden razor, stepped forward, and shaved several tracks across the monster’s crown. She gave him a “Mount Tai Pressing on the Summit,” leaving three patches of hair and tying them into three little horn-shaped tufts. Pilgrim laughed at his side. “What dreadful luck for this demon! He has been made neither male nor female—I cannot tell what sort of thing he resembles.” The Bodhisattva said, “Now that you have accepted my precepts, I shall not treat you lightly. How would it be if I named you Sudhana, the Boy of Good Wealth?” The demon nodded and accepted it, thinking only of having his life spared. The Bodhisattva pointed with one hand and cried, “Withdraw!” With a clatter, all the Heavenly Stems’ blades fell away into the dust, leaving the boy’s body unharmed.

p.src: Now the boy’s wild nature was still unsettled. Seeing that the places where his legs had hurt no longer hurt, that his torn buttocks were no longer torn, and that his hair had merely been tied into three tufts, he strode over, snatched up his spear, and said to the Bodhisattva, “What true divine power did you have to subdue me? It was nothing but a trick to deceive the eye. I will accept no precepts. Take this!” He thrust the spear straight at the Bodhisattva’s face. Pilgrim was so enraged that he swung up his iron staff to strike. The Bodhisattva merely called, “Do not strike him. I have my own means of punishing him.” She drew another golden fillet from her sleeve and said, “This treasure is one of the three fillets—the Golden, the Constricting, and the Prohibitive—which our Buddha the Tathagata bestowed upon me when I went to the Eastern Land to seek the scripture pilgrim. The Constricting Fillet was placed upon you first; the Prohibitive Fillet was used to take in the mountain-guarding deity; but I had never been willing to give this Golden Fillet to anyone. Now I see how insolent this monster is, so I shall give it to him.” The good Bodhisattva held the fillet up to the wind, gave it a shake, and cried, “Transform!” It instantly changed into five fillets. She tossed them toward the boy and shouted, “Fasten!” One encircled the crown of his head, two closed around his left and right wrists, and two around his left and right ankles. The Bodhisattva said, “Wukong, move aside a little while I recite the Golden Fillet Spell.” Pilgrim panicked. “Bodhisattva! I asked you here to subdue the demon. Why are you going to cast a spell on me?” The Bodhisattva replied, “This is not the Constricting Fillet Spell that binds you. It is the Golden Fillet Spell that binds that boy.” Only then was Pilgrim reassured. He stayed close at her side and listened as she recited the spell. The Bodhisattva formed a ritual sign with her fingers and silently recited the spell several times. The demon clutched his ears, rubbed his cheeks, drew up all four limbs, and rolled upon the ground.
